To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

an atypical cross‐reacting immunological component in serum can invalidate the erythropoietic radioimmunoassays, that this cross‐reacting component can be separated from erythropoietins, and that it can be detected by gel‐filtration chromatography.

(a) the serum of two out of 130 normal children had invalid erythropoietins radioimmunoassays; (b) the serum samples were found to contain an erythropoietic cross‐reactant that was eluted before the normal human and recombinant human forms of erythropoieitn on gel filtration chromatography; (c) this cross‐reactant may be an immunologically cross‐reactive protein in the serum; and (d)

(1) the serum from two out of 130 children had an invalid RIA response; (2) the invalid response was due to nonparallelism with the IRPe; (3) a cross‐reactant in the sera was eluted before normal erythropoetin and the 125I marker; (4) the cross‐reactant is probably a protein, and (5) the cross‐ reactant is immunogenic.

the identification of a serum immunological cross‐reaction of erythropoiesis which may invalidate the RIA.
the development of a new, sensitive, and specific radioimmunoassays (RIA) for human erythropoiein.
the development of a radioimmunoassays for erythropoietic hormones.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the RIA response dilution lines of serum samples from normal children may be non‐parallel with the IRP, and the RIA may be invalid.
